Issued at 414 PM CDT Fri Oct 30 2026

-- FORECAST CHANGES OF NOTE/BIG PICTURE COMMENTS/PRIMARY
 UNCERTAINTIES:

As evidenced by the fairly lengthly list of KEY MESSAGES above,
our weather pattern remains quite active. On a positive note, 
although bringing more beneficial rain (at least longer term 
beneficial) with most of our forecast area (CWA) very generally 
expected to receive at least 1-2" of rain between tonight and 
Tuesday, in the shorter-term this pattern is obviously wreaking
havoc for those trying to wrap up/continue harvest. For those
folks, HOPEFULLY the latter half of next week continues to
maintain its current MOSTLY dry look. 

As for key forecast uncertainties...
- Of note in the very short term: Will at least patchy dense fog
  impact our northern counties (mainly north of I-80) overnight? 

- Looking into early next week: certainly the "highlight" of the
  entire 7-day forecast right now is to what degree we are
  impacted by the large-scale/strong/deep low pressure system
  mainly Sunday night-Tuesday. While widespread rain and
  moderately-strong winds (both ahead of and behind it) are
  looking increasingly likely, what is still a SOMEWHAT-
  CONCERNING UNKNOWN is whether (or not) we see a round of
  strong to perhaps severe thunderstorms along the advancing
  cold front/surface low pressure system Monday afternoon-early
  evening? At this time, various models (ECMWF/GFS/NAM) suggest
  that both instability and perhaps to some degree deep-layer
  shear could be on the lower-end of the spectrum for any kind
  of "higher end" severe storm threat, but these trends bear
  close watching. At least for now, SPC has kept it's 15 percent
  "slight risk equivalent" area slightly south-southeast of our
  CWA on the latest Day 4 (Monday) severe storm outlook, but
  tools such as CSU machine learning severe probs currently
  paint at least low chances within primarily the eastern half
  of our CWA. Obviously these details will surely come into
  better focus over the weekend and Monday nears. 


-- 7-DAY FORECAST CHRONOLOGICAL DETAILS (through Fri. Nov. 6):
- CURRENT/RECENT WEATHER SITUATION AS OF 330 PM:
Overall no big surprises today. In short, the morning saw a
smattering of weak thunderstorms mainly in our far east-central
counties, along with some dense fog in southwesterly counties.
In the wake of these things, much of the late-morning through
mid-afternoon was simply continued cloudy under fairly 
widespread low stratus. However, especially within the last hour
another round of very spotty showers/perhaps a few rumbles of 
thunder have started affecting mainly part of our KS zones, as 
water vapor satellite/short-term model data confirm that the 
leading edge of lift is arriving from the next/incoming upper 
wave lifting our way out of the Southern High Plains/western KS 
area. At the surface, a weak warm front is evident lifting very 
slowly north through our KS zones, with winds to its south 
trying to turn more southerly with time, while most of our CWA 
is reporting light (5-10 MPH) southeast winds north of the 
boundary. High temps on track to top out 60s most areas, but 
ranging from upper 50s far north (Ord area) to low 70s far 
southeast (Thayer/Mitchell/Jewell counties). 

- THIS EVENING-OVERNIGHT:
Sticking to the basics: High confidence in continued widespread
stratus clouds with some patchy drizzle almost anywhere, with at
least isolated-scattered showers/weak thunderstorms also lifting
north into more of our area and possible almost anywhere.
Certainly the MAIN CONCERN overnight is whether fog becomes
dense enough to warrant a possible Advisory...which would seem
most favored to occur within our Nebraska counties
along/especially north of I-80. Given only medium confidence in
truly widespread/truly dense fog development, we've opted to 
hold off for now on any formal Advisory, but fog is obviously 
highlighted as a possible concern here and in our Hazardous 
Weather Outlook (HWOGID). Breezes overnight turn more southerly 
as the warm front lifts north. 

- SATURDAY-SATURDAY NIGHT:
These 24 hours are simply best described as "a varied mix of dry
weather interspersed with passing showers". It's just impossible
to truly guarantee any particular area to remain dry more than a
few hours at a time, given persistent weak lift from the upper 
wave lifting east-northeast through our region. Put another way,
trick-or-treaters should be ready for some passing (mainly 
light) rain showers, just in case. Compared to today, south- 
southeast winds will be a little breezier, with sustained speeds
commonly 10-15 MPH and gusts up to around 20 MPH. High temps 
were largely unchanged with most areas a few degrees either side
of 60 degrees, while lows Saturday night were nudged up 
slightly to mainly low-mid 50s given widespread clouds.
